title: Losing Just One Hour of Sleep Adds Weight in Six Weeks, Study Finds
snippet: Cutting daily sleep by just about one hour and 20 minutes leads to increases in both body weight and waist circumference in as little as six weeks,

Clipart KoreaCutting daily sleep by just about one hour and 20 minutes leads to increases in both body weight and waist circumference in as little as six weeks, according to a new study. The research suggests that insufficient sleep does more than simply extend waking hours—it alters lifestyle habits, such as increasing sedentary time, potentially raising the risk of obesity and metabolic disease.On the 11th, researchers at Columbia University's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons announced that their analysis of a clinical trial involving adults at risk of cardiometabolic disease confirmed that prolonged mild sleep deprivation is associated with weight gain, expanded waist circumference, and increased sedentary behavior. The findings were published in the latest issue of Annals of Internal Medicine, the journal of the American College of Physicians (ACP).The study involved 95 adults aged 20 or older who normally slept seven or more hours per day. Participants maintained their usual sleep for a certain period, then, during another period, delayed their bedtime by 90 minutes, reducing their sleep for about six weeks. A washout period was placed between the two experiments to minimize the influence of prior conditions.The researchers used wrist-worn activity monitors to continuously record sleep and physical activity, and comparatively analyzed changes in body weight, waist circumference, body fat mass, and body composition.As a result, during the sleep-restriction period, participants' actual sleep time decreased by an average of 78.4 minutes per day. Meanwhile, body weight increased by an average of 0.45 kg, and waist circumference increased by an average of 0.52 cm.Changes were also observed in activity levels. Although sleeping less lengthened waking hours, the daily average time spent sitting or barely moving actually increased by 17.2 minutes. In particular, men and postmenopausal women showed a tendency for this sedentary time to increase by up to about 30 minutes per day.The researchers explained that the significance of these results lies in the fact that they reflect chronic sleep reduction at a level actually experienced by many adults, rather than extreme sleep deprivation. Many previous studies were conducted over short periods in extreme conditions that limited sleep to around four hours per day, somewhat distant from reality.Lead author Professor Faris Zuraikat explained, "The weight gained over six weeks may seem small, but if this lifestyle pattern continues for months or years, the cumulative effect may be far from trivial." He added, "Chronic sleep deprivation has the potential to lead to clinically meaningful weight gain over time."Professor Marie-Pierre St-Onge, who led the study, also stressed the importance of sufficient sleep. "The exact physiological mechanism by which sleep deprivation causes weight gain requires further research, but the results show that the less sleep one gets, the higher the potential risk of obesity-related diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease," she said.She added, "Weight management and cardiometabolic disease prevention programs need to consider strategies that help maintain sufficient sleep, not just diet and exercise," and said, "Follow-up research on the long-term health benefits of improving sleep should also continue."#SleepHealth#WeightGain#SleepDeprivation#Obesity#Metabolism#HealthyLiving#MedicalResearchOriginal reporting by Lim Hye-rin for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
